If skimming, the generalized Feynman-Kac correctors paper (composing and steering diffusion models) is the most foundational, and the landmark pick, Neural ODEs (2018), underpins the continuous-time flows behind flow matching and Boltzmann generators.

landmark.title: Neural Ordinary Differential Equations
landmark.abstract: We introduce a new family of deep neural network models. Instead of specifying a discrete sequence of hidden layers, we parameterize the derivative of the hidden state using a neural network. The output of the network is computed using a black-box differential equation solver. These continuous-depth models have constant memory cost, adapt their evaluation strategy to each input, and can explicitly trade numerical precision for speed. We demonstrate these properties in continuous-depth residual networks and continuous-time latent variable models. We also construct continuous normalizing flows,
landmark.worth_30_min: NeurIPS 2018 best paper. It recasts deep networks as continuous-time dynamics solved by black-box ODE solvers. It also introduced continuous normalizing flows through the instantaneous change-of-variables formula, with adjoint-based gradients at constant memory. That idea is the direct ancestor of flow matching, the probability-flow ODE view of diffusion, and equivariant continuous flows used in Boltzmann generators and crystal generative models.
landmark.inspiration: Flow-based samplers could propose molecular crystal packings, such as lattice parameters plus rigid-molecule poses, with exact likelihoods. These proposals could seed or replace GA initial pools (a Genarris analogue). Likelihoods allow reweighting toward a Boltzmann distribution at DFT-ranked energies. Continuous flows also suggest learned mutation/crossover operators: transport a parent structure along a learned vector field instead of applying random perturbations.
landmark.foundations: The ODE view of residual networks. The adjoint sensitivity method for backpropagating through solvers. The instantaneous change of variables (density change equals the trace of the Jacobian) and Hutchinson-style trace estimation, which FFJORD later used. Trade-offs of adaptive solvers. The conceptual bridge from discrete normalizing flows to continuous ones, which flow matching later trains without simulation.
landmark.reading_guide: Read the intro and Sec 2 on the adjoint method, including Fig 2 (10 min). Then read Sec 4 on continuous normalizing flows: the theorem on instantaneous change of variables and the planar-flow comparison figures (12 min). Skim Sec 3 (MNIST experiments) and Sec 5 (latent time series). Spend the remaining time sketching how flow matching replaces maximum-likelihood ODE training.

items.title: Composing and Steering Diffusion Models with Generalized Feynman-Kac Correctors
items.abstract: Diffusion models have become the leading paradigm in generative modeling, yet many applications require sampling from distributions that are not those of any single pretrained model, but are instead defined through combinations of several models, possibly tilted toward high values of a downstream reward. Naively combining the scores of the models yields incorrect samples, while existing corrections are restricted to specific families of targets. In this work, we introduce the generalized Feynman-Kac correctors (GFKC), a principled framework for sampling from an arbitrary target function of several pretrained diffusion models. We show that the geometric interpolation between an arbitrary initial function and the target function of the models satisfies a Feynman--Kac partial differential equation, and derive its potential in closed form. To evaluate this potential during generation, we further generalize the log-probability ODE to track the density of each model along trajectories driven by a different velocity field. The resulting algorithm operates entirely in the log domain, incorporates reward-based steering at no additional conceptual cost, and corrects the generation on the fly

items.title: WASABI: Wasserstein Sampling via Bridge Interpolants
items.abstract: Sampling from Boltzmann distributions is a fundamental problem in physics, chemistry, and biology. We introduce WAsserstein SAmpling via Bridge Interpolants (WASABI), a method that trains a diffusion model to generate samples from a target Boltzmann distribution given access only to the energy function. WASABI minimizes the KL divergence between the distribution generated by its diffusion model and the Boltzmann target using Wasserstein gradient flows. This approach builds on a principle underlying classical sampling methods such as Langevin dynamics. However, applying Wasserstein gradient flows to diffusion models is challenging because the updates require the gradient of the model's own log density, which is generally intractable. We derive a practical training algorithm that avoids computing this gradient. Once trained, WASABI can generate new samples without further evaluations of the energy or its gradient. On alanine dipeptide, WASABI outperforms the best reported baselines using an estimated 3.3 times fewer energy evaluations. It also achieves competitive performance on interacting particle system benchmarks.

items.title: EVA-Flow: Learning Shared Chemistry for Unified Environment-Aware Molecular Conformation Generation
items.abstract: Molecular 3D structures underpin simulations of thermodynamics, kinetics, crystallization, and nucleation, making their accurate prediction central to drug discovery and materials design. However, molecular geometry can change dramatically across environments. Existing models either ignore environmental effects or train separate models for each environment. We hypothesize that transfer learning across contexts is possible for conformer generation and that a general model will perform better when training data are limited, as in ligand binding and crystallization. We introduce EVA-Flow, a unified framework for environment-aware molecular conformation generation that learns shared chemical structure and adapts it through environment-conditioned generative modeling. Across vacuum, protein-ligand docking, solvation, and crystal packing, pretraining and cross-environment finetuning provide their largest gains in the three data-scarce settings. Evaluation against multiple reference conformations shows that EVA-Flow covers a broad range of solvation conformations. Analyses of molecules shared across environments support its ability to generate different conformations for the same molecule

items.title: AtomSteer: Test-Time Constraint Steering for Atomistic Generative Models
items.abstract: Diffusion and flow matching models offer scalable approaches to generating crystalline materials, molecular conformers, and protein-ligand complexes. However, satisfying crystallographic symmetry, structural geometry, and accurate stereochemistry remains challenging. Satisfying these requirements calls for corrections that preserve the geometry already captured by the pretrained model. In this work, we propose AtomSteer, a test-time inference framework for steering pretrained atomistic generative models with structural constraints. During sampling, AtomSteer corrects intermediate structure predictions with bounded local projections, graph-rigid stereochemical transformations, and projections over periodic symmetries, accepting updates that improve constraint satisfaction while limiting changes to the rest of the structure. We demonstrate AtomSteer across three pretrained backbones, FlowMM, ET-Flow, and Boltz-2, spanning de novo crystal generation and crystal structure prediction, molecular conformer generation, and protein-ligand complex structure prediction. AtomSteer improves space-group distribution coverage in de novo crystal generation and improves target space-group recovery

items.title: Rigorously Certified Neural-Network Computation of Nonlinear Water Waves at Near-Machine Precision
items.abstract: We present a computational framework that combines machine-learning-based discovery with rigorous computer-assisted numerical certification and formal verification for strongly nonlinear partial differential equations. We demonstrate the approach for periodic gravity-capillary traveling water waves. Physics-informed neural networks are used as a search mechanism, with the wave profile, wave speed and, in continuation experiments, surface tension learned directly from the governing equations without training data. Through a staged training and refinement procedure, the neural networks achieve near-machine-precision residuals of the governing equations, even in strongly nonlinear regimes. A single formulation recovers high-amplitude Stokes waves, Crapper waves and Wilton ripples. Continuation from a high-amplitude Wilton ripple in surface tension reveals new high-amplitude candidate solutions. We freeze one candidate as an explicit finite representation and rigorously certify a uniform bound on its governing-equation residual using interval arithmetic, accounting for floating-point roundoff, Fourier truncation, aliasing and grid-to-continuum errors. items.title: Ab initio simulation of excited-state potential energy surfaces with transferable deep quantum Monte Carlo
items.abstract: Abstract The accurate quantum chemical calculation of excited states is a challenging task, often requiring computationally demanding methods. When entire ground and excited potential energy surfaces (PESs) are desired, for instance, to predict the interaction of light excitation and structural changes, one is often forced to use cheaper computational methods at the cost of reduced accuracy. Here we introduce a method for the geometrically transferable optimization of neural network wavefunctions that leverages weight sharing and a dynamical ordering of electronic states. Our method enables the efficient prediction of ground- and excited-state PESs and their intersections at the highest accuracy, demonstrating up to two orders of magnitude cost reduction compared with single-point calculations. We validate our approach on four challenging excited-state PESs, namely, ethylene, the carbon dimer, the methylenimmonium cation and a rubredoxin active site model containing 96 electrons, illustrating the potential of transferable deep-learning quantum Monte Carlo as a practical framework for studying electronic excitations in molecules.

rubric.why: Solid Noe-group advance in deep QMC excited states, but incremental within the neural-wavefunction line and far from MCSP needs; not landmark tier.

items.summary: Transferable neural-network wavefunction (deep QMC) optimization across geometries for excited states, via weight sharing and dynamic state ordering; claims ~100x cost reduction vs single-point runs, including conical intersections.
